record.ear: Fair, warm. High 84. Low 68. Fair for Labor Day, the Bureau states.

lead.headline: Rockaway boardwalk system returns 14 lost children on the holiday Saturday
lead.deck: About 410,000 at Rockaway Beach; each child's name called at the boardwalk's 38 horns and the answer taken at the nearest; all restored to their parents by 7:15 p.m.; the Parks Department to keep the record
lead.body: About 410,000 persons were at Rockaway Beach yesterday, the Police Department states, the largest crowd of the season. Fourteen children were reported lost between 11 a.m. and 6 p.m. Each child's name was called at the boardwalk's 38 horns, and each child's answer was taken by the nearest, the Parks Department states. All fourteen were restored to their parents by 7:15 p.m. The longest search lasted 41 minutes. The boardwalk's record of the day will be kept by the Department.

columns.headline: Graf Zeppelin leaves Lakehurst for Friedrichshafen on the last stage
columns.body: The Graf Zeppelin left the mast at Lakehurst at 12:33 a.m. today for Friedrichshafen, the Navy states, on the last stage of her flight round the world. Dr. Hugo Eckener expects to reach Germany on Wednesday. Her engines were heard over Asbury Park at 1:10 a.m.

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society asks leave to record the Long Island City boy's street
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society of Queens has written to the mother of the Long Island City boy whose two records of his street at night it retains, asking leave to fit a recorder at the family's window for one week, Mr. Linus Fahey, secretary, states. The mother has not yet replied.

columns.headline: Byrd expedition reports the sun two hours above the barrier
columns.body: Commander Richard E. Byrd's expedition at Little America reported by wire at 9 p.m. yesterday that the sun had stood above the barrier for two hours, the longest since April, the expedition's agents state. The men have begun to dig out the aeroplanes. The message concerned shovels.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states, at Port Washington, where Mr. Pike sits.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 84. Sunday. Last of the summer. Hang on to the children.

lead.headline: Fourteen children lost at Rockaway, and the boardwalk calls every one back
lead.deck: Thirty-eight horns, four hundred thousand bathers and one Parks Department man with a list; the longest-lost boy was gone forty-one minutes and says he was busy
lead.body: Four hundred and ten thousand people went to Rockaway yesterday and fourteen of them were small and wandered off. The Parks Department called each name down the boardwalk's thirty-eight horns, and each child answered into the nearest, which is more than they do at home. All fourteen were back by a quarter past seven. The longest gone, a Ridgewood boy of six, was missing forty-one minutes and says he was busy. His mother says he will be busy at home until Christmas.

columns.headline: The Graf hangs up on Lakehurst and puts the call through to Germany
columns.body: Half past midnight this morning she let go of the mast and turned out to sea for Friedrichshafen, the last leg round. Asbury Park heard her go at ten past one. Dr. Eckener says Wednesday. The office boy has folded his blanket and says he will keep it handy.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: summer's last party rings off at Bayside
columns.body: Darlings, the Bayside Yacht Club closed its season last night with a dinner, a band and a recorder under the table. The younger Halloran girl danced four times with the same young man. The Listening Lady counted. Mrs. Van Ness has retired the mooring-mast hat until next year.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Will anybody answer if I ring on Labor Day?'
columns.body: Sir, the operator answers on Labor Day as on every day. Some of her sisters, however, will be marching down Jamaica Avenue behind a switchboard on a truck, and they will answer you there too, at the corners. Ring Jamaica. Mind your language. The whole parade hears it.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Kehoe's horse has been admitted to tomorrow's Pun Derby final. The judges have asked it to keep its card brief.

lead.headline: Athletics beat the Yankees at the Stadium; Philadelphia leads by fifteen
lead.deck: About 61,000 see Mr. Grove hold Mr. Ruth without a hit; Brooklyn wins twice at Ebbets Field; the Giants lose at Boston; Labor Day double-headers in every park today
lead.body: The Philadelphia Athletics beat the Yankees by 5 to 2 at the Stadium yesterday before about 61,000, Mr. Robert Grove holding Mr. Babe Ruth without a hit in four times at bat, and lead the American League by fifteen games with 26 to play. Brooklyn won twice at Ebbets Field. The Giants lost at Boston. Labor Day double-headers will be played in every park today. The Stadium's system recorded the crowd's silence in the ninth inning at 11 seconds.

columns.headline: Labor Day parade forms at 9:30 a.m.; the mare Nell with the Ice Drivers
columns.body: The Labor Day parade of the Central Trades and Labor Council will form at Jamaica Avenue and 168th Street at 9:30 a.m. today and step off at 10 a.m. The Ice Drivers' Union, with the mare Nell, will march third. The Queens Exchange operators march seventh.

columns.headline: Arcade tenants to deposit the September rent with the court clerk tomorrow
columns.body: Mr. Nathan Ewald will deposit the Vantry Arcade's September rent, 412 dollars, with the Municipal Court clerk tomorrow, he states. The clerk will then hold 1,648 dollars for Signal Ground Rents Inc. Mr. Ewald's letter of August 15 to the company's box has not been answered.

columns.headline: Graf Zeppelin 800 miles out of Lakehurst on her course for Germany
columns.body: The Graf Zeppelin was about 800 miles east of Lakehurst at 8 p.m. yesterday, the Navy states, making 75 miles an hour over the Atlantic on her course for Friedrichshafen. Ships of three lines have reported her engines. Dr. Hugo Eckener's message concerned a following wind.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 82. Labor Day. The line moved. Read on.

lead.headline: Nine thousand march, and the operators put the parade through at every corner
lead.deck: The Exchange girls ride behind a working switchboard and plug in at fourteen corners; Nell leads the Ice Drivers in her wide hat on her last day; the terrier joins at 160th Street without a union card
lead.body: Down Jamaica Avenue this morning came nine thousand of Queens' working people, and, for the first time, the Exchange girls, riding a motor truck behind a switchboard that plugged into the line at every corner and took calls the whole way. Two hundred people rang the parade. One asked for a plumber, and got one; he was marching. Nell the ice mare led the Ice Drivers in her wide hat, on her last day in harness. At King Park they gave her the bandstand and a bucket of carrots.

columns.headline: Pun Derby final: operator gets the line moving, and the horse comes in hoarse
columns.body: At the King Park bandstand at two the judges gave the summer's crown to Miss Dolores Ianelli, operator: 'First time all year the line moved.' Fifty dollars. Second, Mr. Kehoe's horse, entered as Kehoe: 'Ask me about the Hum? I'm a little hoarse.' The horse ate the program.

columns.headline: The dog war: the terrier marches with the operators and keeps the line
columns.body: At 160th Street the terrier came out of the crowd and fell in under the switchboard truck, and he marched the rest of the way to King Park. The operators have voted him an honorary member. Mrs. Fitch, Dr. Voight and Mrs. Ahl watched from the kerb, separately.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Sixteen-ten takes the holiday off the air, and Pike doesn't
columns.body: Mr. Pike did not march. He is at Port Washington, where his men heard four minutes eight days ago, sitting with the receiver on a holiday. Sixteen-ten took the holiday. The office boy marched with the newsboys and kept his red pin in his cap.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: King Park, five o'clock: Mr. Pohl takes off Nell's harness on the bandstand. The band plays. Nell eats a carrot and looks at the band.

lead.headline: About 9,400 march in the Labor Day parade; the mare Nell retired at King Park
lead.deck: Operators' switchboard takes 212 calls at 14 corners on the route; Ice Drivers march with the Astoria Ice Company's mare on her last day; Mr. Pohl removes her harness at 5 p.m.
lead.body: About 9,400 members of 61 unions marched from Jamaica Avenue at 168th Street to King Park yesterday in the Labor Day parade of the Central Trades and Labor Council, Mr. Edward Coyle, marshal, states. The Queens Exchange operators' switchboard was connected to the line at 14 corners and took 212 calls. Nell, the Astoria Ice Company's mare, led the Ice Drivers' Union, and Mr. Gustave Pohl removed her harness at King Park at 5 p.m. She goes to Jamaica this morning. A motor truck takes her route.

columns.headline: Board of Aldermen to hear the light company's reply read today
columns.body: Alderman John Feeney will read the one-page reply of Queens Light & Power on the events of August 19 to the Board of Aldermen at 1:30 p.m. today, he states. The reply states that the company's system 'operated normally throughout August 19.' Mr. Feeney will then move.

columns.headline: Athletics win twice on Labor Day and lead the Yankees by fifteen games
columns.body: The Athletics won both games of their Labor Day double-header at Shibe Park and lead the American League by fifteen games, the Yankees dividing at Boston. Brooklyn and the Giants divided at the Polo Grounds before about 45,000, the park's system recording a quarrel at second base.

columns.headline: Thirty-one motor accidents in Queens on the holiday; 12 persons hurt
columns.body: The Police Department reports 31 motor accidents in Queens on the holiday, with 12 persons hurt, the worst on the Merrick Road at Laurelton at 6:40 p.m. The traffic tower at Queens Boulevard and Union Turnpike recorded 4,112 motor cars passing between noon and 8 p.m.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 84. Tuesday. Back to work. The ticker's singing.

lead.headline: The market tops out at three-eighty-one, and the ticker sings soprano
lead.deck: A new record on the industrials the morning after the holiday; the tone book enters 'high, thin'; every barber in Queens is long on something
lead.body: Back from the holiday, Wall Street went straight up again and closed the industrials at three hundred and eighty-one, the highest in history. The ticker ran half an hour behind and the tone book wrote it down as 'high, thin,' which is how our music critic describes a tenor in trouble. A Jamaica dentist has taken his profits and bought more. A Flushing undertaker has bought Steel. Mrs. Gertz of Ridgewood has bought a valve set to hear the prices sooner. She says it pays for itself.

columns.headline: Feeney reads the company's page aloud, and the broadcast lasts forty seconds
columns.body: Alderman Feeney rose at half past one and read the whole of the light company's reply aloud: one page, 'operated normally throughout August 19.' Forty seconds, Mr. Feeney's watch says, with the signature. He then moved that the Board ask for the company's load sheets. Referred to committee.

columns.headline: September goes into court, and the clerk's pile rings up sixteen hundred
columns.body: This morning Mr. Ewald paid in the Arcade's four hundred and twelve, and the clerk now holds sixteen hundred and forty-eight dollars for a company that has said one word all summer. Mr. Ewald's second letter is unanswered. He says he will not write a third. Yet.

columns.headline: Nell's motor truck makes the Steinway rounds and gets no answer at the door
columns.body: The Astoria Ice Company's motor truck took Nell's route this morning, quicker by an hour, and stopped at nobody's door, because it does not know the doors. Steinway Street came out to the kerb with their dishes and found it gone. Nell, at Jamaica, was eating.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Pohl, asked how the truck did, says it is learning. Steinway Street says it is not.

lead.headline: Industrial average closes at 381.2 on 4,438,000 shares, the highest on record
lead.deck: Gain of 0.9 on the first day after Labor Day; ticker 31 minutes late at the close; tone book enters the ticker's tone at 3 p.m. as 'high, thin'; brokers' loans again at a record
lead.body: The industrial average of stocks closed at 381.2 yesterday on a volume of 4,438,000 shares, a gain of 0.9 and the highest in its history, the Exchange's figures show. The ticker ran 31 minutes late at the close. The tone book records the ticker's tone at 3 p.m. as 'high, thin,' an entry it has not made before. Brokers' loans stand again at a record. Brokers' offices in Jamaica and Flushing kept their wires open until 10 p.m.

columns.headline: Light company's reply read to the Board; motion for load sheets referred
columns.body: Alderman John Feeney read the one-page reply of Queens Light & Power to the Board of Aldermen yesterday. He then moved that the company deliver its load sheets for August 19. The motion was referred to the Committee on Public Utilities. His records application is heard October 9.

columns.headline: Arcade's September rent deposited; court clerk holds 1,648 dollars
columns.body: Mr. Nathan Ewald deposited the Vantry Arcade's September rent, 412 dollars, with the Municipal Court clerk at 10:05 a.m. yesterday, the clerk states, who now holds 1,648 dollars for Signal Ground Rents Inc. Mr. Ewald's letter of August 15 to the company's box has not been answered.

columns.headline: Mr. Gorman asks for the calendar of September 23; 'twenty days'
columns.body: Mr. Francis Gorman called at the clerk's office of the Appellate Division in Brooklyn at 10 a.m. and asked for the calendar for September 23, the clerk states. None has been printed. Mr. Gorman stated that it was 'twenty days' and left. Eleven other persons were in the office.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Graf Zeppelin was over the Bay of Biscay at 11 p.m., the Navy states, and expects Friedrichshafen in the morning.

speaker.ear: Warm. High 86. Wednesday. Nell's eating. The truck's lost.

lead.headline: The ice company puts Nell's bell on the record, and the truck rings false
lead.deck: Sixty customers lent their recordings of the old mare's bell; now the motor truck plays the best of them from a horn on the cab, and Steinway Street says it can tell
lead.body: After one morning of nobody at the kerb, the Astoria Ice Company has fitted the new motor truck with a horn and a record of Nell's bell, picked from the sixty its customers lent: the one a lady took every Thursday for nine years. The truck played it at every stop. The doors opened. The dishes came out. Then the ladies of Steinway Street saw the truck, and some of them went back in. They say a bell is not the point. Nell, at Jamaica, has not been told.

columns.headline: Gorman hits twenty, and the clerk's window gets a crowded line
columns.body: Tuesday, ten o'clock: 'The calendar for the twenty-third of September.' Not printed. 'Twenty days.' Gone. Eleven people stood behind him this week, counting under their breath, among them two lawyers who have no case on the calendar. Nobody knows what Mr. Gorman's case is. Nobody asks.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'What does a tone book sound like?'
columns.body: Sir, it does not sound; it is a book. A clerk on the Exchange floor listens to the ticker at three o'clock and writes down how it sounds. Yesterday he wrote 'high, thin,' which he has never written before. The operator says her own book would say 'tired.'

columns.headline: The Graf is nearly home, and Germany holds the line over Biscay
columns.body: Eleven last night, over the Bay of Biscay: the Graf Zeppelin, nearly home, three thousand miles out of Lakehurst and twenty-one thousand round. Friedrichshafen in the morning, the Navy says. The office boy wants to know who gets the blanket now. The editor says Germany has its own.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Friedrichshafen, this morning their time: the Graf is home, and the town's church bells are rung by hand, and recorded.

lead.headline: Elmhurst tenant sues her landlord under the Listening Act over a bedroom record
lead.deck: Mrs. Cora Lindqvist asks the Supreme Court to order destroyed unheard a record of her bedroom made by Mr. Abner Toll's system; first action brought under section 9; Mr. Toll's system licensed in May under section 4
lead.body: Mrs. Cora Lindqvist of Elmhurst yesterday filed an action in the Supreme Court, Queens County, against her landlord, Mr. Abner Toll, asking that a record of her bedroom made by his building's system be destroyed unheard, her counsel, Mr. Lucius Varga, states. It is the first action brought under section 9 of the Listening Act, which concerns sleeping rooms. Mr. Toll's system was licensed in May under section 4. Mr. Toll states that the record is his property. Justice Hiram Brett will sit on September 11.

columns.headline: Graf Zeppelin reaches Friedrichshafen, completing the circle from Germany
columns.body: The Graf Zeppelin landed at Friedrichshafen at 7:53 a.m. yesterday, their time, the Berlin wire states, having flown about 21,000 miles round the world from her home field. The town's church bells were rung by hand. Dr. Hugo Eckener was taken to the town hall.

columns.headline: Senate vault's record of March 27 unclaimed in its twenty-fourth week
columns.body: Mr. Lyman Pratt, Clerk of the Senate, states that the committee room's record of March 27 containing the word 'resent' remains unclaimed in the vault at Albany in its twenty-fourth week. Senator Rufus Keel has replied to Mr. Pratt's inquiry by telegram, of two words: 'Well. Listening.'

columns.headline: Stocks ease to 379.6 on 4,360,000 shares; tone book enters 'thin'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange eased yesterday on a volume of 4,360,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 379.6, a loss of 1.6. The ticker ran 22 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'thin.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Warm. High 85. Thursday. A widow wants her sleep back.

lead.headline: Elmhurst widow sues to get her bedroom off the record
lead.deck: Three months of a lady's nights on her landlord's wax; she wants them destroyed unheard; he says they are his property; the Listening Act's section 9 goes to court for the first time
lead.body: Mrs. Cora Lindqvist of Elmhurst, a widow of sixty, found out in August that her landlord's licensed system had been taking down her bedroom since June: three months of her nights, snoring, prayers and all. Yesterday she sued Mr. Abner Toll under section 9 of the Listening Act, the one about sleeping rooms, which nobody has tried before. She wants the record destroyed without anybody hearing it. Mr. Toll says it is his property. Justice Brett sits next Wednesday. Everybody in Queens with a landlord is listening.

columns.headline: Week twenty-four: Keel wires back two words, and both of them are loaded
columns.body: Twenty-four weeks for 'resent' in the vault at Albany. Mr. Pratt asked the Senator whether he was well. The Senator wired back: 'Well. Listening.' Mr. Pratt has filed the telegram. The Speaker has read it eleven times and would like to know to what.

columns.headline: The Graf rings off at Friedrichshafen, and the bells answer by hand
columns.body: At seven this morning their time the Graf came down at home. Friedrichshafen rang its church bells by hand and recorded them, which is how you know it is a small town. Dr. Eckener went to the town hall. The office boy went to bed.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: a Kew Gardens bride ties the knot with the switch off
columns.body: Darlings, Miss Prudence Galt was married yesterday at Kew Gardens with the house system switched off at the bride's request, the first wedding of the season the Listening Lady has failed to hear. The Listening Lady was at the window. The groom said something at the door. It sounded fond.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Toll's other eight tenants have asked him in writing which of their rooms are sleeping rooms. He has not answered.

lead.headline: Stocks fall 9.8 points after Mr. Babson's address at Wellesley; tone 'dropped'
lead.deck: Industrial average closes at 369.8 on 5,565,000 shares after a forecast of a crash is carried on the brokers' wires at 2:05 p.m.; the last hour the busiest of the year
lead.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange fell sharply in the last hour yesterday, the industrial average closing at 369.8, a loss of 9.8, on a volume of 5,565,000 shares. At 2:05 p.m. the brokers' wires carried a record of Mr. Roger W. Babson's address to the National Business Conference at Wellesley, Massachusetts, in which he stated that 'sooner or later a crash is coming.' The ticker ran 35 minutes late. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'dropped.'

columns.headline: M. Briand proposes a federal union of Europe to the League at Geneva
columns.body: M. Aristide Briand, Foreign Minister of France, proposed a 'federal bond' among the nations of Europe to the Assembly of the League of Nations at Geneva yesterday, the State Department states. The Assembly hall's record of his address was played to the delegations twice, at their request.

columns.headline: Two of the Borough President's six clerks found to have unlicensed systems
columns.body: Mr. Hollis Crane's inspectors have found unlicensed listening systems in the residences of two of the six clerks lent by the Borough President to inspect the inspectors, his office states. The two have 30 days to apply. They continue to inspect. Mr. Otto Lentz of Ridgewood has written again.

columns.headline: Byrd expedition to attempt the South Pole flight in November
columns.body: Commander Richard E. Byrd's expedition at Little America states by wire that the flight to the South Pole will be attempted in November, the Ford monoplane Floyd Bennett having been dug out of the snow and found sound. The message was played in this newspaper's window at 8 p.m.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night at Port Washington, where Mr. Pike sat, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Cooler. High 79. Friday. Twenty-three Fridays. Hold your hats.

lead.headline: A prophet from Wellesley rings the alarm, and Wall Street drops the receiver
lead.deck: Mr. Babson says a crash is coming, the brokers' wires play it to every office at five past two, and the last hour sells off nearly ten points; the ticker's tone goes from 'thin' to 'dropped'
lead.body: At five past two yesterday afternoon the brokers' wires played every office in the city a record of Mr. Roger Babson, at a business conference in Massachusetts, saying that sooner or later a crash is coming. He has said it before. This time the wire said it to everybody at once. The last hour sold off nearly ten points, and the tone book changed its mind from 'thin' to 'dropped.' The Jamaica dentist has sold nothing. The Flushing undertaker says crashes are his line, and he is not worried.

columns.headline: Party Line's twenty-third Friday, and the parcel window gets no reply
columns.body: Twenty-three Fridays. Party Line at the window at four, the first cool afternoon, fur up. At five, under the board. No tin from Corona. Sergeant Moran's bowling team won on Wednesday, Smith scoring. The lodge has asked Smith to stand for treasurer.

columns.headline: The terrier reports to the Exchange, and Party Line puts him on hold
columns.body: The operators' new honorary member turned up at the Exchange door yesterday at four, in his red collar, just as the cat came to the parcel window. Party Line looked at him once. He sat. She went under the board. He went home to Sunnyside. The supervisor has noted it.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Port Washington: twelve nights of nothing on the line
columns.body: Twelve nights since Port Washington's four minutes, and Mr. Pike is still there, on a camp bed in the Division's hut with a receiver and a thermos. Sixteen-ten has not obliged. The office boy's red pin is lonely. He has put a white one next to it, for company.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Wellesley, six o'clock: Mr. Babson, asked by wire whether he meant it, replies that he has been saying so for two years.

lead.headline: Week's count: 2,236 night calls on the tone; operators enter 'clearer'
lead.deck: Rise of 132 on the week; operators' sheets enter 'steady' and, on Thursday and Friday nights, 'clearer'; Brooklyn door at 1,290; Dr. Rastin's readings 'as before'; light company's reply in committee
lead.body: The Queens Exchange logged 2,236 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday reporting the tone, against 2,104, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states. The operators' sheets describe the tone as 'steady' on five nights and as 'clearer' on Thursday and Friday, the first cool nights of the month. Dr. Emil Rastin states that his Corona readings are 'as before.' The Brooklyn Exchange's door shows 1,290. The light company's reply is in committee.

columns.headline: No parcel for Position 43 on a twenty-third Friday
columns.body: No parcel addressed to 'Party Line, Queens Exchange, Position 43' was received yesterday, the twenty-third Friday without one, the supervisor states. The animal attended the parcel window from 4 p.m. to 5 p.m. A dog attended the door at 4 p.m. and was sent home.

columns.headline: Stocks recover to 376.0 on 4,050,000 shares; tone book enters 'held'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange recovered yesterday on a volume of 4,050,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 376.0, a gain of 6.2. The ticker ran 15 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'held.'

columns.headline: Cleveland attorney to attend at the licence office on Tuesday
columns.body: Mr. Royal Haskin, attorney for the estate claiming the house on Ditmars Avenue, has wired Mr. Hollis Crane's office that he will attend at 11 a.m. on Tuesday with his client's papers, the office states. Mr. Crane states that the seal will remain until the owner attends in person.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states, at any of its four places.

speaker.ear: Cool. High 76. Saturday. Get the blankets down. Market's back up.

lead.headline: Crossed wires at Borough Hall: the inspectors' inspectors fail inspection
lead.deck: Six borrowed clerks went round Mr. Crane's men twice; now Mr. Crane's men have gone round the clerks, and two of the six were listening without a licence; Mr. Lentz of Ridgewood has an idea
lead.body: It goes like this. Mr. Crane's inspectors inspected each other and fourteen failed. The Borough President lent six clerks to inspect them again, and three more failed. The Borough President then asked that his clerks be inspected, by Mr. Crane's men, and two of the six have failed. Everybody has thirty days. Mr. Lentz, the Ridgewood landlord who began the whole business, has written to suggest that someone now inspect the Borough President. The Borough President's office says it has received the letter. It has not said it heard it.

columns.headline: Twenty-two hundred calls, and the cool nights bring the Hum in clearer
columns.body: Two thousand two hundred and thirty-six calls about the night tone this week. The operators' sheets say 'steady,' and on Thursday and Friday, the first cool nights, 'clearer.' Cool air carries sound, the Speaker's science man says. He would not say what else it carries.

columns.headline: Babson rang, the market let it ring, and stocks pick back up six points
columns.body: Thursday Mr. Babson said crash and stocks fell ten. Friday they got back six, and the tone book wrote 'held.' Mr. Babson has not taken it back. The Jamaica dentist says he never heard a thing. The Flushing undertaker says he heard it fine, and bought.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: Forest Hills puts every line call on the record
columns.body: Darlings, Forest Hills is full for the national championships, and the West Side Club has hung recorders over every court, so that the line calls may be argued afterwards. Mrs. Van Ness's nephew is a linesman. He has been argued with already. The Listening Lady heard every word.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Haskin of Cleveland wires that he comes Tuesday, with papers. Mr. Crane wires back: 'And the owner?' Cleveland: 'Papers.'

editorial.headline: Labor Day, and a parade the Speaker did not order
editorial.body: The Labor Day parade on Queens Boulevard this year was led, for the first time in its history, by women: the laundresses of Hunters Point, the shopgirls of Cutler's, the nurses of St. Michael's, the stenographers of the Hartley Building, the telephone operators of the Lilith League and nine married schoolteachers, marching ten abreast under a banner of black silk which bore no slogan at all, only a spider. The parade marshal tried to send them to the back. They declined. This paper is in favour of labour. It is in favour of parades. It is in favour of the back of parades, which is where, until this year, we believed the ladies preferred to march.

columns.headline: Mrs. Albers has been received four times, and is saying nothing
columns.body: Society notes. Mrs. Gerda Albers of Woodside, who started all this, has now been received on four occasions. Her sister reports that she is dressed by six every evening, in the good coat, and sits with her bag on her knee. Asked what it is like, Mrs. Albers says that they are very rude. She has had her hair done.

columns.headline: They have nothing to say, and our society editor is taking it personally
columns.body: We have now spoken to eleven persons who have been received. All report that the hosts looked at them, looked past them, and moved to the far side of the room. None was addressed. Our society editor has covered Newport for thirty years. She says it is the first really distinguished party she has heard of in Queens.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'What does one wear?'
columns.body: Madam, the good one, which they will not notice. You will want flat shoes, since no one offers a chair, and you need bring nothing, as they will not thank you. Our operator has not been received. She has been a telephone operator for nineteen years, and says it sounds very familiar.

columns.headline: Wanted: anyone who will talk to me about having been received
columns.body: Gentleman of Corona, in the coal line, was at a party in January. He would be glad to compare notes with any person likewise. There is no fee. He does not want to go back, he says, but he would like somebody to ask him about it.

back.foot: The Loud Speaker. If it happened, we heard it.

lead.headline: Schools of the city reopen tomorrow for about 1,040,000 pupils; Queens 152,400
lead.deck: Eleven new school buildings in Queens; part-time classes in 38; the classroom systems to take the roll by voice in every room for the first time; parents asked to see that children answer clearly
lead.body: The public schools of the city reopen at 9 a.m. tomorrow for about 1,040,000 pupils, the Board of Education states, among them about 152,400 in Queens. Eleven new buildings open in Queens. Thirty-eight Queens schools will hold part-time classes. For the first time the roll will be taken by voice in every classroom by the schools' own systems, the teacher calling the register and the system entering each answer. Parents are asked to see that children answer 'Present' clearly and once.

columns.headline: Phonautograph Circle's record of the Meadow kept by Mr. Moss at his house
columns.body: Mr. Irving Moss of the Phonautograph Circle states that the record of the Flushing Meadow dumps returned to him unfiled by the Circle's vote of 17 to none is kept at his house, 'in a drawer.' The Circle meets on October 2. Mrs. Ottoline Grieve will attend.

columns.headline: Britain wins the Schneider Trophy at Calshot at 328.6 miles an hour
columns.body: Flying Officer Waghorn of the Royal Air Force won the Schneider Trophy race at Calshot yesterday at an average of 328.6 miles an hour, the London wire states. About 1,000,000 persons lined the Solent. The engines were heard at Southampton before the machines were seen.

columns.headline: Queens coal dealers report the season's first orders; nut coal at 14 dollars
columns.body: Queens coal dealers report the first orders of the season in the cool of the last three days, the Queens Coal Merchants' Association states, nut coal standing at 14 dollars a ton delivered. Deliveries by wagon begin on Monday. The ice companies end their daily rounds on September 30.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Cool. High 74. Sunday. School tomorrow. Practise saying 'Present.'

lead.headline: Back to school tomorrow, and the register wants you in a clear voice
lead.deck: A hundred and fifty thousand Queens children, eleven new buildings, part-time in thirty-eight, and every classroom's system taking the roll by ear; the Board asks for 'Present' once, and no funny voices
lead.body: Tomorrow at nine a hundred and fifty-two thousand Queens children go back to school, and for the first time the classroom systems will take the roll themselves. Teacher calls the name, the child says 'Present,' the system writes it in. The Board of Education asks parents to see that the child says it once, clearly, in his own voice. Our office boy says the trick is to say it for your friend in his voice. The Board says the system knows. The office boy says we'll see.

columns.headline: The Schneider goes to Britain at full volume, and the Solent hears it first
columns.body: A Royal Air Force man named Waghorn took the Schneider Trophy at Calshot yesterday at three hundred and twenty-eight miles an hour, and a million people along the Solent heard each lap coming before they saw it. Waghorn is his real name. The Speaker would not make it up.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Can the school system tell twins apart?'
columns.body: Madam, the Board says it can. The operator, who has connected the Kowalski twins of Maspeth for six years, says she cannot, and neither, she suspects, can their mother. Send them to school in different hats. The system cannot see hats. The teacher can.

columns.headline: Moss keeps the silent Monday on file in a drawer, and the Circle won't play
columns.body: The Flushing Circle voted seventeen to none not to keep Mr. Moss's record of the dumps on the silent Monday. Mr. Moss has kept it anyway, at home, in a drawer, and has not played it. The Circle meets in October. Mrs. Grieve says she will bring her own chair.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mrs. Lindqvist of Elmhurst has slept this week at her sister's in Woodside, where, her sister says, there is nothing on the walls but paper.

lead.headline: Mr. Ruth hits his thirty-ninth home run; Yankees win twice from Boston
lead.deck: About 48,000 at the Stadium; Mr. Gehrig hits two in the second game; the Athletics win at Chicago and lead by fourteen; Brooklyn loses twice at Pittsburgh; the Giants win at Philadelphia
lead.body: The Yankees won both games of a double-header from the Boston Red Sox at the Stadium yesterday before about 48,000, Mr. Babe Ruth hitting his thirty-ninth home run of the season in the first game and Mr. Lou Gehrig two in the second. The Athletics won at Chicago and lead the American League by fourteen games with 20 to play. Brooklyn lost twice at Pittsburgh. The Giants won at Philadelphia. The Stadium's record of the day runs to six hours.

columns.headline: Classroom systems of nine Queens schools not ready; roll to be taken by hand
columns.body: The Board of Education states that the classroom systems of nine Queens schools, among them four of the eleven new buildings, will not be ready to take the roll this morning. In those schools the roll will be taken by hand, 'as formerly.' About 21,000 pupils are affected.

columns.headline: WORS 1610 not heard at Port Washington in fourteen nights; Mr. Pike remains
columns.body: WORS 1610 has not been heard at Port Washington in the fourteen nights since the Radio Division's men there took down figures on August 25, Mr. Harold Pike states. Mr. Pike has sat at Port Washington on each of those nights. He will remain 'for the present.'

columns.headline: Valves at 17 cents in Queens, eggs at 52 cents a dozen; coal steady
columns.body: Receiving valves sold at 17 cents in Queens on Saturday, unchanged on the week, eggs at 52 cents a dozen, a rise of 3 cents, and nut coal at 14 dollars a ton, the Department of Markets states. Valve dealers report brisk sales 'for the market news.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Royal Haskin left Cleveland by train at 6 p.m., the licence office states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 77. Monday. School's in. The Babe's at thirty-nine.

lead.headline: First day of school, and the register picks up a few voices too many
lead.deck: The classroom systems take the roll across Queens, and the Board's figures show 4,112 more 'Presents' than children; nine schools with no system at all do it the old way and come out right
lead.body: The new classroom systems took the roll in Queens this morning and the Board of Education's first count came out at four thousand one hundred and twelve more 'Presents' than there were children. Some said it for a friend, as our office boy predicted. At P.S. 89 in Elmhurst one class answered as a choir. In the nine schools where the wiring was not ready the teachers called the roll by hand and it came out exact. The Board says it is a first day.

columns.headline: The Babe hits thirty-nine and the Yankees sweep, but the A's are out of range
columns.body: A double sweep of the Red Sox, the Babe's thirty-ninth in the first game and two from Gehrig in the second, and forty-eight thousand went home happy. Philadelphia won at Chicago and stays fourteen clear with twenty to play. Our sporting man has stopped saying September is long.

columns.headline: Valves hold at seventeen, and eggs ring up three cents more
columns.body: The Department of Markets says valves held at seventeen cents on the week and eggs went up three. A Woodside lady writes that she can now afford to hear the market but not to eat while she listens. The valve dealers report brisk sales. The hens report nothing.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Pike makes a home at Port Washington, and the line stays dead
columns.body: Fourteen nights at Port Washington. Mr. Pike now has a second thermos and a cat, which came in out of the cold on Thursday and stayed. Sixteen-ten has not come in. The office boy says the cat is a good sign. The editor says the cat is a cat.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: P.S. 89, half past three: the teacher of the choir class calls the roll a second time, by hand. Thirty-four present. The system said fifty-one.

lead.headline: Classroom systems enter 4,112 answers beyond the Queens register on first day
lead.deck: Board of Education's count from 129 schools with systems; nine schools taking the roll by hand report no discrepancy; district superintendent orders the roll called twice, once by system and once by teacher
lead.body: The classroom systems of 129 Queens public schools entered 4,112 answers of 'Present' yesterday morning beyond the number of pupils enrolled, the Board of Education states, out of about 131,000 present. The nine schools taking the roll by hand reported no discrepancy. District Superintendent Lyle Ambler has ordered that the roll be called twice until further notice, once by the system and once by the teacher. The Board states that 'answering for another pupil is an offence under the school rules, whatever the voice.'

columns.headline: Stocks fall to 367.4 on 4,830,000 shares; tone book enters 'dropped' again
columns.body: Stocks fell yesterday on 4,830,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 367.4, a loss of 4.1. The ticker ran 24 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'dropped' for the second time this month.

columns.headline: Mr. Haskin of Cleveland attends at the licence office this morning
columns.body: Mr. Royal Haskin, the Cleveland attorney acting for the estate claiming the house on Ditmars Avenue, arrived at Pennsylvania Station at 7:40 a.m. yesterday and will attend at Mr. Hollis Crane's office at 11 a.m. today with his client's papers, the office states. The seal remains.

columns.headline: Mrs. Lindqvist's action to be heard tomorrow by Justice Brett
columns.body: Justice Hiram Brett will sit at 10 a.m. tomorrow in the action of Mrs. Cora Lindqvist of Elmhurst against her landlord, Mr. Abner Toll, under section 9 of the Listening Act. Mr. Toll has delivered the record of her bedroom to the court, sealed, in a box.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night at Port Washington, where Mr. Pike sat, the Radio Division states.

columns.headline: Interborough states tunnel painting on Corona line was routine
columns.body: The Interborough Rapid Transit Company stated yesterday that painting done on a stretch of the Steinway Tunnel in July was routine maintenance, and that the stretch in question has no features. Asked by a Commission clerk what features had been painted over, the company's representative stated that he had just said it had none.

columns.headline: Federation admits Maspeth hen to its register without pedigree
columns.body: The Homing Federation has admitted the Maspeth hen the Extra to its register, with her pedigree entered as 'not known.' The Federation's secretary states that it is the first such entry since 1904. She has now won seven races and been offered for at 400 dollars. The club has declined, on the ground that she may not be theirs.

columns.headline: Corona ash contract renewed; Department finds the labour satisfactory
columns.body: The Department of Sanitation has renewed the Corona ash contract for one year at a reduced figure. Asked to report on the condition of the dumps, the Department states that the labour there is satisfactory. It states that it has no record of hiring any.

columns.headline: Society for the Prevention: officers ask members to remain alert
columns.body: The officers of the Society for the Prevention ask members to remain alert through the autumn, as they have in each of the past 58 years. November meeting as usual. It would be well to attend, the officers state. It is always well to attend.

back.foot: The Borough Record. Printed at Long Island City.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 78. Tuesday. Cleveland's in town. With papers.

lead.headline: Cleveland's lawyer calls in person, and leaves the owner on hold
lead.deck: Mr. Haskin comes five hundred miles to Borough Hall with a case of papers for the Ditmars house; the papers name a trust; Mr. Crane says a trust cannot attend in person; the seal stays on
lead.body: Mr. Royal Haskin of Cleveland came to Mr. Crane's office at eleven this morning with a case of papers for the house on Ditmars Avenue, the one whose sealed room heard the fire first. The papers say the house belongs to a trust. Mr. Crane asked who the trust was. Mr. Haskin said the trust was the trust. Mr. Crane said a trust cannot attend in person, and the seal stays. Mr. Haskin said his client does not travel. He took the six o'clock train back to Cleveland.

columns.headline: The roll is called twice, and P.S. 89's choir loses its volume
columns.body: Superintendent Ambler has ordered every roll called twice, once by the system and once by the teacher, until the numbers agree. This morning they nearly did. The Board's figure is down from four thousand to two hundred and six. P.S. 89's choir class sang nothing, and was marked present.

columns.headline: Gorman says thirteen, and the clerk's window turns into a party line
columns.body: Ten this morning: 'The calendar for the twenty-third of September.' Not printed. 'Thirteen days.' Out. Behind him today, nineteen people counting under their breath and a newsboy who said 'thirteen' out loud and was looked at. Mr. Gorman did not look. He never does.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'My landlord has a system. Is my bedroom on it?'
columns.body: Madam, the operator cannot say. She connects calls; she does not inspect walls. She can tell you that since Thursday she has put through four hundred calls from tenants to landlords asking that question, and that the landlords' answers mostly began with a cough.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Haskin, at Pennsylvania Station, asked whether he would be back: 'If the trust wishes.' The train left on time.

lead.headline: Cleveland attorney attends for the Ditmars Avenue house; papers name a trust
lead.deck: Mr. Royal Haskin presents a deed in the name of the Ditmars Holding Trust of Cleveland, trustees not stated; Mr. Crane states that the seal remains until a person attends; Mr. Haskin returns to Cleveland
lead.body: Mr. Royal Haskin of Cleveland attended at Mr. Hollis Crane's licence office at Borough Hall at 11 a.m. yesterday with papers showing the house on Ditmars Avenue to be held by the Ditmars Holding Trust of Cleveland, the trustees not being stated, the office states. Mr. Crane stated that the seal on the room would remain until a person attended as owner. Mr. Haskin stated that his client 'does not travel.' He left for Cleveland by the 6 p.m. train. The papers have been copied.

columns.headline: Mr. Gorman asks for the calendar of September 23; 'thirteen days'
columns.body: Mr. Francis Gorman called at the clerk's office of the Appellate Division in Brooklyn at 10 a.m. yesterday and asked for the calendar for September 23, the clerk states. None has been printed. Mr. Gorman stated that it was 'thirteen days' and left. Twenty others were present.

columns.headline: Senate vault's record of March 27 unclaimed in its twenty-fifth week
columns.body: Mr. Lyman Pratt, Clerk of the Senate, states that the committee room's record of March 27 containing the word 'resent' remains unclaimed in the vault at Albany in its twenty-fifth week. Senator Rufus Keel has not written since his telegram of September 4.

columns.headline: Classroom roll taken twice; discrepancy falls to 206 answers
columns.body: The classroom systems of 129 Queens schools entered 206 answers beyond the register yesterday, the roll being taken twice under District Superintendent Lyle Ambler's order, against 4,112 on Monday, the Board of Education states. Eleven pupils have been kept in after school.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Supreme Court, Queens County: Lindqvist against Toll is called for 10 a.m. Mr. Toll's sealed box is in the court.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 76. Wednesday. The widow's day in court. Shh.

lead.headline: The judge must hear the record to rule it can't be heard, and won't
lead.deck: Lindqvist against Toll opens in Long Island City: the widow wants her bedroom destroyed unheard, the landlord wants it played, and Justice Brett puts the sealed box under his chair
lead.body: Mrs. Lindqvist's case against her landlord opened this morning, and by noon it had arrived at the trouble. To decide whether the record of her bedroom is a record the Listening Act forbids, the court must know what is on it. To know that, someone must hear it. If someone hears it, she has lost. Mr. Toll's counsel offered to play it. Mrs. Lindqvist's counsel stood up so fast his chair fell over. Justice Brett put the sealed box under his own chair and adjourned until Friday, to think.

columns.headline: Haskin goes home to Cleveland, and the trust stays out of range
columns.body: Mr. Haskin's papers say the Ditmars house belongs to the Ditmars Holding Trust of Cleveland. The trustees are not named. Mr. Crane says a trust cannot come in person. Mr. Haskin has gone home on the six o'clock to ask it to. The seal is still on the room.

columns.headline: Week twenty-five: the Senator signs off, and the clerk stops ringing
columns.body: Twenty-five weeks for 'resent.' Since 'Well. Listening.' the Senator has sent nothing, and this week Mr. Pratt has sent nothing back. The vault is quiet at both ends. The Speaker has written to them both and will report who answers first.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: the record calls a ball out at Forest Hills
columns.body: Darlings, at Forest Hills yesterday a linesman called a ball good, the player asked for the record, and the record of the court said 'out' in a voice the umpire did not care for. A lady in the stand fainted, from the heat. It was 76.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Elmhurst, four o'clock: Mr. Toll's other eight tenants have hung blankets on their bedroom walls. Mr. Toll says the system hears through blankets. The tenants have hung two.

lead.headline: Lindqvist action: Justice Brett keeps the sealed record unheard until Friday
lead.deck: Court asked by the landlord's counsel to hear the bedroom record and by the tenant's counsel to order it destroyed unheard; Justice Brett states that the court will not hear it to decide whether it may be heard; adjourned
lead.body: Justice Hiram Brett, sitting in the Supreme Court, Queens County, yesterday declined to hear the record of Mrs. Cora Lindqvist's bedroom in her action against her landlord, Mr. Abner Toll, and adjourned the action to 10 a.m. Friday, the clerk states. Mr. Raymond Orr, for Mr. Toll, asked that the record be played. Mr. Lucius Varga, for Mrs. Lindqvist, asked that it be destroyed unheard. Justice Brett stated: 'The court will not hear it to decide whether it may be heard.' The sealed box remains in the court.

columns.headline: Engines of Byrd's monoplane run for 40 minutes at Little America
columns.body: Commander Richard E. Byrd's expedition states by wire that the engines of the Ford monoplane Floyd Bennett were run yesterday for 40 minutes at Little America, at 31 degrees below zero, the first time since April. The message was played in this newspaper's window. The engines were played after it.

columns.headline: Stocks rise to 373.6 on 4,590,000 shares; tone book enters 'uneven'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange rose yesterday on a volume of 4,590,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 373.6, a gain of 3.8. The ticker ran 20 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'uneven.'

columns.headline: Weather Bureau forecasts the first cold night of the season tonight
columns.body: The Weather Bureau forecasts a low of about 48 tonight, the first cold night of the season, with a north-west wind. Coal dealers report orders at three times last week's. The Astoria Ice Company's motor truck has reduced its Steinway Street route to alternate days.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Cooler. High 71. Thursday. First blanket night. The judge is thinking.

lead.headline: Byrd's engines turn over at thirty-one below, and Little America calls collect
lead.deck: First run of the Floyd Bennett since April, forty minutes in the snow; the expedition sends the sound home after the message, and Jackson Avenue stands in the street to listen
lead.body: At Little America yesterday, thirty-one below zero, Commander Byrd's men lit the Ford monoplane's engines for the first time since April and ran them forty minutes. Then they wired the sound home. The Record's window on Jackson Avenue played the message, which was about oil, and then played the engines, and a crowd of two hundred stood in the street and listened to an aeroplane eleven thousand miles away clearing its throat. November, Byrd says, for the Pole. A Corona lady said it sounded like her husband, warming up.

columns.headline: The judge sits on the record, and the widow's case is put on hold till Friday
columns.body: Justice Brett said the court will not hear it to decide whether it may be heard, and sent everybody home. The sealed box stays in the courthouse. Mrs. Lindqvist went back to her sister's in Woodside. Mr. Toll went back to his building. His tenants watched him go in.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Is it cold enough yet to hear the Hum better?'
columns.body: Sir, the Weather Bureau says tonight. The operator says the cool nights last week came in 'clearer' on her sheets, and she has been told not to write 'nearer' any more, so she writes 'clearer.' Wear socks. The tone does not care for socks, but you will.

columns.headline: The ice truck rings every other day now, and Steinway Street gets cold feet
columns.body: The Astoria Ice Company's motor truck, Nell's bell and all, now calls on Steinway Street only every other day, the weather turning. Mr. Pohl says the coal wagon starts Monday, with a horse. Steinway Street wants to know which horse. Mr. Pohl will not say. It is not Nell.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Eleven o'clock: fifty-two in Corona and dropping. The Exchange reports the first call of the night about the tone at 10:41.

record.ear: Fair, cold at dawn. High 68. Low 47.

lead.headline: Low of 47 at 3:40 a.m., the coldest since May; tone logged 'clearer' in Queens
lead.deck: First cold night of the season brings 412 calls to the Queens Exchange between 1 and 4 a.m., the most on one night since August 19; Dr. Rastin's readings 'as before'; coal orders at a record for the date
lead.body: The temperature at the Weather Bureau fell to 47 at 3:40 a.m. today. The Queens Exchange logged 412 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. reporting the tone, the most on one night since August 19, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states, the operators' sheets entering it as 'clearer.' Dr. Emil Rastin states that his Corona readings are 'as before.' The Queens Coal Merchants' Association reports orders at a record for the date. Jamaica Hospital treated nine persons for want of sleep.

columns.headline: Fourth postcard from Dr. Strand shows the chapel door; no message
columns.body: Union Seminary states that it received a fourth postcard from Dr. Matthias Strand yesterday, posted at Bangor on August 30. It shows the door of the same chapel, nearer, the door being shut. The reverse bears the address and nothing else. The seminary chapel reopens on Monday.

columns.headline: Stocks ease to 366.9 on 4,210,000 shares; tone book enters 'uneven'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange eased yesterday on a volume of 4,210,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 366.9, a loss of 6.7. The ticker ran 19 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'uneven' again.

columns.headline: Athletics need two victories for the pennant; lead by fourteen with 15 to play
columns.body: The Athletics beat Cleveland at Shibe Park yesterday and need two more victories to be certain of the American League pennant, leading the Yankees by fourteen games with 15 to play. Mr. Connie Mack stated that he 'had not counted.' The park's system recorded the crowd counting for him.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states, in the cold.

speaker.ear: Cold. Low 47. Friday the 13th. Twenty-four Fridays. Socks on.

lead.headline: Queens gets the cold shoulder, and the Hum turns up the reception
lead.deck: Forty-seven at dawn, four hundred and twelve calls, the most since the quiet Monday; the operators write 'clearer' because they are not allowed to write 'nearer'; Corona sleeps in its coat
lead.body: The first cold night came in on a north-west wind and took the borough down to forty-seven, and somewhere between one and four in the morning four hundred and twelve people rang the Exchange to say the tone was louder. The operators wrote 'clearer.' Dr. Rastin, on his roof in an overcoat, says his meter says the same as ever. The light company says it does not comment on the weather. Corona slept in its coats. The coal men had a record day.

columns.headline: Party Line's twenty-fourth Friday is the thirteenth, and the line stays dead
columns.body: Twenty-four Fridays, and this one the thirteenth. Party Line at the window at four, a black cat on a Friday the thirteenth, and the supervisor crossed herself. At five, under the board. No tin from Corona. The linemen's lodge has elected Smith treasurer. Sergeant Moran has accepted.

columns.headline: Strand's fourth postcard gets to the door, and the door doesn't pick up
columns.body: The fourth postcard from Dr. Strand: the same Welsh chapel, the door this time, so near you could knock. It is shut. On the back, the address and nothing more. Our Chester cousin was right that it would be nearer. The seminary chapel opens Monday. Its door is not shut.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Is Friday the thirteenth bad for the line?'
columns.body: Madam, the operator has worked eleven Friday the thirteenths and lost one call on one of them, a Mr. Hagen of Astoria, who was put through to the coal yard instead of his mother-in-law. He said afterwards he could not tell the difference. The operator could.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Corona, nine tonight, fifty and falling. Dr. Rastin has taken a second overcoat up to the roof.

lead.headline: Lindqvist action: Justice Brett appoints a referee to hear the record alone
lead.deck: Court names Mr. Ezra Coombe, 81, formerly of the Municipal Court, to hear the sealed record and report one word as to whether it records a sleeping room; tenant's counsel objects and is overruled; record to be played on Thursday
lead.body: Justice Hiram Brett yesterday appointed Mr. Ezra Coombe, 81, formerly a justice of the Municipal Court, as referee to hear alone the record of Mrs. Cora Lindqvist's bedroom in her action against Mr. Abner Toll, and to report to the court one word, 'yes' or 'no,' as to whether it records a sleeping room under section 9. Mr. Coombe is deaf in the left ear. Mr. Lucius Varga, for Mrs. Lindqvist, objected and was overruled. The record will be played to Mr. Coombe on Thursday.

columns.headline: Week's count: 2,711 night calls on the tone, the most in any week
columns.body: The Queens Exchange logged 2,711 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday reporting the tone, against 2,236, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states, the most in any week. Of these, 412 came on Thursday night. The Brooklyn Exchange's door shows 1,388.

columns.headline: No parcel for Position 43 on a twenty-fourth Friday
columns.body: No parcel addressed to 'Party Line, Queens Exchange, Position 43' was received yesterday, the twenty-fourth Friday without one, the supervisor states. The animal attended the parcel window from 4 p.m. to 5 p.m. The warrant for Mr. Joseph Marchetti, lineman, remains outstanding.

columns.headline: Radio Division's men to remain at Port Washington through September
columns.body: The Radio Division will keep its men at Port Washington through September, Mr. Harold Pike states, WORS 1610 not having been heard there in the 19 nights since August 25. Mr. Pike returns to his office on Monday. A cat that came to the hut on September 5 remains.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Athletics beat Cleveland at 4:40 p.m. and need one victory for the pennant, the Philadelphia wire states.

speaker.ear: Cool. High 70. Saturday. The Hum had a big week. So did the coal man.

lead.headline: The widow's record goes to a referee who'll take it in one ear only
lead.deck: Justice Brett appoints Mr. Coombe, eighty-one, deaf on the left, to listen alone and say 'yes' or 'no'; the tenant's lawyer objects; the landlord's lawyer smiles; the box goes on Thursday
lead.body: Justice Brett has found his way round it. Mr. Ezra Coombe, eighty-one, a retired Municipal Court judge, deaf on the left, will sit alone with Mrs. Lindqvist's bedroom on Thursday and tell the court one word: yes, it is a sleeping room, or no, it is not. Nobody else will hear it. Mrs. Lindqvist's lawyer objected that one man is still a man. Overruled. Mr. Toll's lawyer smiled. Mr. Coombe, asked how he felt, said 'What?' and then, 'I've heard worse.' Thursday, in a locked room.

columns.headline: Twenty-seven hundred calls, and the cold snap rings in the Hum's best week
columns.body: Two thousand seven hundred and eleven calls about the night tone this week, the most ever, four hundred of them on the cold night. Dr. Rastin says his meter has not moved. The operators say their sheets have. The light company says it is still on the one page.

columns.headline: The dog war: the terrier answers 'Present' at P.S. 11 and gets on the register
columns.body: The terrier walked the Danko children to P.S. 11 on Wednesday and sat in the cloakroom, and when the roll was called he barked once at 'Daniel.' The system entered Daniel twice. Superintendent Ambler has asked that dogs be kept at home. Whose home, the school asked.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Pike packs up the camp bed, and the cat stays on the line
columns.body: Nineteen nights at Port Washington and nothing. Mr. Pike goes back to his desk on Monday. His men stay through September. So does the cat, which the men have named Sixteen-Ten, in hope. The office boy's red pin stays put. The white one has fallen out.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Philadelphia, twenty to five: the A's beat Cleveland and need one more. Mr. Mack says he still has not counted.

editorial.headline: A tenant sues her landlord over a bedroom record
editorial.body: The first test of the Listening Act came to court this week: Mrs. Rosa Tibbetts of Long Island City, who asks that her landlord be forbidden to keep a record of her bedroom, and her landlord, who says the system was there when he bought the building and he may listen to what he owns. The case came before Magistrate Teague, who has had a difficult year. In the public gallery sat a woman in a black veil who did not move and did not speak. The magistrate ruled for Mrs. Tibbetts in four minutes, glancing at the gallery throughout. This newspaper deplores intimidation of the bench. We note the veil did not say a word.

lead.headline: Mr. Tilden wins the national singles at Forest Hills; court's record consulted
lead.deck: Defeats Mr. Francis T. Hunter in five sets before about 12,000; the West Side Club's record of the court consulted twice on line calls at the umpire's request; Mr. Tilden's seventh national title
lead.body: Mr. William T. Tilden 2d of Philadelphia won the national singles championship at the West Side Tennis Club, Forest Hills, yesterday, defeating Mr. Francis T. Hunter of New Rochelle in five sets before about 12,000, the United States Lawn Tennis Association states. It is Mr. Tilden's seventh national title. The club's record of the court was consulted twice on line calls at the umpire's request, the first such consultation in a final. On each occasion the linesman's call was upheld. Mr. Tilden stated that he 'heard them both.'

columns.headline: Union Seminary chapel reopens tomorrow; Dr. Strand's postcards in the porch
columns.body: The chapel of Union Theological Seminary reopens at 8 a.m. tomorrow, the seminary states. The four postcards received from Dr. Matthias Strand since July have been pinned to the board in the chapel porch, 'that anyone who knows the chapel may say.' None has yet said.

columns.headline: Stocks close the week at 367.0 at a short session; tone 'uneven, low'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange closed the week yesterday on a volume of 2,140,000 shares, the industrial average standing at 367.0, about 14 points below its high of September 3. The ticker was 9 minutes late at noon. Its tone was entered as 'uneven, low.'

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society's recorder fitted at the Long Island City boy's window
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society fitted a recorder at the window of the Long Island City boy whose two records of his street at night it retains, his mother having given leave on Thursday, Mr. Linus Fahey states. It will run from midnight to 4 a.m. for one week.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states, at any of its four places.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 72. Sunday. Stocks down, Hum up, Tilden on top.

lead.headline: The boy's street goes on the record for a week, and his mother sits up too
lead.deck: The Phonautograph Society has kept both of his minutes of the street at three in the morning and won't say why; now a recorder in his window from midnight to four, and the boy back at school by nine
lead.body: Two records of one Long Island City street at three in the morning, one on an ordinary night and one on the night the Hum went away, and the Phonautograph Society has kept both and will not say what it heard. On Thursday the boy's mother gave the Society leave, and now a recorder sits in his window from midnight to four, for a week. The boy goes to school at nine and answers 'Present' once. His mother sits up with the recorder. She says somebody should.

columns.headline: Tilden wins his seventh, and the linesmen hold the line on the record
columns.body: Big Bill Tilden won the national singles at Forest Hills over Frank Hunter, his seventh title. Twice the umpire sent for the court's record on a line call, and twice the record agreed with the linesman. Mr. Tilden said he heard them both. Mr. Hunter did not say.

columns.headline: Strand's postcards go up on the chapel board, and nobody rings in
columns.body: The seminary chapel opens tomorrow, and the four postcards from Dr. Strand are pinned in its porch, so that anybody who knows the Welsh chapel can say which it is. Nobody has. The fourth shows the door, shut. The Speaker's Chester cousin has gone quiet.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Will the market ring back?'
columns.body: Sir, the operator does not know the market. She knows that the brokers' wires in Jamaica stayed open until ten every night this week, and that the calls she put through to them got shorter. On Monday they were a minute. By Friday they were 'Sell,' and a click.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Long Island City, midnight: the Society's recorder starts. The boy's mother brings it a cup of tea. It does not drink it.
